title: Nordic-led frontier AI control call now backed by 32 states and the European Commission
subtitle: Ahead of Monday's Bridgetown summit, Norway and Finland's push to coordinate frontier-model oversight has drawn broader state backing than Macron's earlier Paris Call.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: A frontier-AI control initiative led by Norway and Finland is now signed by 32 states and the European Commission, organizers said ahead of a hybrid summit in Bridgetown on Monday. The call sits alongside — and overtakes in signatory count — the Paris Call for AI Safety and Security that Emmanuel Macron rolled out at the Élysée on November 9. That earlier call was endorsed by roughly 17 governments and 10 AI developers, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft, with the United States notably absent from the official list. Monday's meeting is expected to draw about 150 participants, including Norwegian and Finnish ministers and industry representatives.

The two documents cover similar ground — fail-safe shutdown, incident reporting, shared risk evaluations — but the Bridgetown call deliberately avoids military applications, putting it in a different lane from the CCW process that just ended in Geneva without binding autonomous-weapons rules. Civilian frontier models and battlefield systems are drifting into separate regulatory tracks, each run by a different coalition. Whether those tracks eventually join or diverge is one of the open questions of the next year of AI governance.

The strategic context: Washington still has no federal frontier-AI statute, California is building a state-level framework with 48-hour incident reporting and shutdown authority, New York's RAISE Act takes effect January 1, and Oregon has sued OpenAI for $2.035 billion over teen safety. Into that patchwork, a Nordic-led multilateral call with EU backing is the closest thing to a unified external posture outside the U.S. — which may be precisely why 32 governments have signed and more are expected.

A note for learners: a signature on a 'call' is cheap. What matters is the enforcement scaffolding each signatory actually ships — audit authority, pre-deployment evaluation, incident disclosure that is more than an honor system. When Bridgetown ends, look for the countries that commit to a specific review body with budget and headcount. Those are the real signatories. The rest are marketing.
